passage.excerpt: At the time of the Emperor Hadrian the heresiarchs arose to plague the Church. Saturninus came from Antioch and Basilides from Alexandria. From that time the so-called Gnostic heresy spread like a pestilence. Basilides feigned loftier mysteries and procured the downfall of many in Alexandria; he taught that Christ had not truly suffered but that Simon of Cyrene was substituted and crucified. Saturninus taught that the Saviour was unborn and bodiless, appearing only in the semblance of a man.

passage.excerpt: Valentinus adapted the principles of the heretical school called Gnostic to his own peculiar character of school. He affirmed that in the invisible and ineffable heights there exists a perfect, pre-existent Aeon — Proarche, Propator, and Bythus — invisible and incomprehensible. With him was also Ennoia, whom he calls Charis and Sige. This Bythus, at last resolving to send forth from himself the beginning of all things, deposited this production as a seed in the womb of Sige. The result was Nous and Aletheia — the beginning of a vast pleroma of divine emanations.

object_entity.proposition_label: Faith is transmitted through apostolic succession

passage.excerpt: Hegesippus, in his five Memoirs, states that on a journey to Rome he met many bishops along the way and received the same doctrine from all of them. At Rome he compiled a succession list and remained through the episcopate of Anicetus. He found the same law, the prophets, and the Lord preached everywhere.
